## Overview {#sec-overview}

Tobacco usage has been found to be linked to numerous medical diseases and conditions, one of which is poor oral health \[[1](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/health-effects-tobacco-use/how-tobacco-use-affects-oral-health)\]. The primary objective of this project is to explore the potential association that smoking has on periodontal disease among adults. It will include tobacco use trends in Philadelphia to highlight public health awareness at the local level. The data that will be used for this project comes from a 2011-12 NHANES database on the periodontic aspect of oral health through the R package “ForCausality”.

Dr. Kei Katsura, a Post Doc at CHOP, and Dr. Mohammad Abukar, a professor at Temple University Dental School, were both consulted to aid with identifying potential topics and the types of analyses to be done with the dataset. I also learned a great deal about how secondhand inhalation of smoking can cause an increased risk in oral health problems.

Repo Link: <https://github.com/DannyTran0/BMIN5030_Final_Project>

## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Periodontal disease is a broad condition where bacterial infections and/or inflammatory responses affect gum and bone tissues surrounding and supporting teeth \[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/oral-health/about/gum-periodontal-disease.html)\]. While it can be preventable, it can be destructive if left untreated \[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/oral-health/about/gum-periodontal-disease.html)\]. There are numerous factors that can cause periodontal disease, but this project will focus on the use of tobacco in smoking. Due to the nature of tobacco being burned while smoking, it has been linked to negatively impacting oral health among other health complications \[[1](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/health-effects-tobacco-use/how-tobacco-use-affects-oral-health)\]. Non-smokers are also affected through secondhand smoke exposure which increases risk of health complications especially among children and the elderly \[[3](https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/about/index.html)\]. 

Despite trends in the smoking rate decreasing nationally between 2012-2022 among adults, Philadelphia has consistently remained above the national rate \[[4](https://www.phila.gov/media/20250114150429/CHARTe9v2a_Tobacco-Trends.pdf)\]. Public health support and resources are needed to educate the residents on the dangers of smoking. In turn, smokers would be able to find the help needed to quit smoking.

This project aims to explore the potential association between smoking and periodontal disease measurements among adults. In particular, it will explore how various demographic factors and the number of cigarettes smoked per day is correlated with causing periodontal disease. This is where the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data for 2011-12 comes into play to aid with the analysis. Additionally, it will examine tobacco use in Philadelphia to provide context on the local level with public health.

The project is interdisciplinary as it connects various fields on the issue of smoking as a cause for periodontal disease, including dentistry, biomedical data science, public health, behavioral psychology, and sociology. As such, reaching out to experts in these fields is essential to understand the problem. The following experts were consulted:

- Dr. Kei Katsura: During our conversations, she helped me with formulating and refining my research topic for the project while also describing how I could utilize the different variables to aid with analyzing the data. She had mentioned that due to the “race” variable being too broad, I should be cautious with the conclusions being made as it does not state other races.

- Dr. Mohammad Abukar: During our conversation, we discussed ways to go about analyzing the dataset, suggesting tying in how age, gender, race, and income could cause an individual to turn to smoking and subsequently getting periodontal disease. He also suggested the possibility that I use the analyzed data to apply it to the city of Philadelphia to see which areas are more prone to tobacco use and make a case for spreading awareness about smoking dangers.

## Methods {#sec-methods}

Two datasets will be used for this project. The primary dataset, which assess the number of periodontal disease measurements based on if the participant in a smoker, is from the 2011-12 NHANES on oral health (periodontal) conducted by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). All of the data will be used. The other dataset is from the 2014 and 2017 Census Tract-level Data of 500 U.S. cities provided from the CDC's Division of Population Health, Epidemiology and Surveillance Branch. Model-based estimates on smoking use from Philadelphia and its geographical coordinates data will be used.

#### Package Requirements

Starting off, it is important to install the necessary R packages for use. Below is code that installs the R package `ForCausality` which contains the primary dataset that this project will be using. Including `ForCausality`, various other R packages will be called to aid in analyzing and visualizing the data.

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE

install.packages("ForCausality")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-packages

library(ForCausality)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(modelsummary)
library(sf)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(tidycensus)
library(leaflet)
library(ggspatial)
library(tigris)

options(tigris_use_cache=T)
```

#### Processing of Periodontal-Smoking Data

First, the primary dataset will be loaded into a variable through a function called "Periodontal_df."

```{r}
#Loads primary dataset
periodontal.data<-Periodontal_df
#Views dataset
head(periodontal.data)
```

Despite the package providing processed data, most of it are vague and do not have much meaning. As such, it will be modified to provide proper meaning to the data, one example being the conversion of 0 and 1 from the gender variable to indicate male and female. Smoker status will also be converted and age will be categorized into various age groups. Additionally, the majority of the variable names will be renamed.

```{r}
#Data modifications
periodontal.data<-rename(periodontal.data, #Renames variables to provide more concrete meaning to what data means
                         id=SEQN,
                         gender=female,
                         race=black,
                         education=educf,
                         peri.detected=either,  #Counted number of detected periondontal disease measurements per participant
                         peri.not.detected=neither, #Counted number of no detected periodontal disease measurement per participant
                         percent.peri.detected=pcteither,
                         smoker.status=z,
                         pair=mset) |>
#Modifies and categorizes gender data
  mutate(gender=factor(gender,levels=c(1,0),
                       labels=c("female","male"))) |>
#Modifies and categorizes age data
  mutate(age=case_when(                       
    age>=30 & age<40 ~ "30-40",
    age>=40 & age<50 ~ "40-50",
    age>=50 & age<60 ~ "50-60",
    age>=60 & age<70 ~ "60-70",
    age>=70 & age<80 ~ "70-80",
  )) |>
#Modifies and categorizes race data
  mutate(race=factor(race,levels=c(1,0),      
                     labels=c("African American","Other"))) |>
#Modifies and categorizes smoker status data
  mutate(smoker.status=factor(smoker.status,levels=c(1,0),  
                              labels=c("Smoker","Non-Smoker")))

#Previews dataset to view modifications
head(periodontal.data)
```

#### Upload of Census Tract Data and Consolidation with Periodontal-Smoking Data

For the 2014 and 2017 census-tract data, it will be loaded in through a GitHub link from the data uploaded onto the repository. The data contains a lot of unnecessary data and will have to be filtered to contain data on smoking prevalence ("CSMOKING_CrudePrev") only in the city of Philadelphia. Census tract data such as FIPS code ("TractFIPS") will also be used for selected.

The "tracts" function from the `tigris` package is utilized to select and load in the geospatial coordinates ("GEOID" and "geometry" variables) for Philadelphia from 2014 and 2017, respectively. The smoking prevalence and geospatial coordinate data is merged by using the GEOID/TractFIPS data.

```{r}
#Reads 500Cities_2014_CensusTractData.csv file
smoking.data.2014<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DannyTran0/BMIN5030_Final_Project/refs/heads/master/500Cities_2014_CensusTractData.csv")

#Previews data
head(smoking.data.2014)

#Filters and selects relevant variables
philly.smoking.2014<-smoking.data.2014 |>
  filter(StateAbbr=="PA", PlaceName=="Philadelphia") |>
  mutate(TractFIPS=str_pad(as.character(TractFIPS),
                         width = 11)) |>
  select(TractFIPS,CSMOKING_CrudePrev)

#Variable meaning
#StateAbbr: Abbreviation of U.S. state
#Place Name: Name of U.S. city
#TractFIPS: Designated FIPS code for an area of the cities
#CSMOKING_CrudePrev: 2014 data of smoking prevalence in a particular area of each city

#Checks that everything has been correctly done
head(philly.smoking.2014)
dim(philly.smoking.2014)
```

```{r}
#Loads in 2014 tract data of Philadelphia
philly.tract.2014<-tracts(state="PA",
                          county="Philadelphia",
                          year=2014) |>
  select(GEOID,geometry)

#Merges the geospatial coordinates from the 2014 tract data into smoking data using GEOID
philly.2014<-philly.tract.2014 |>
  inner_join(philly.smoking.2014,
             by=c("GEOID"="TractFIPS"))

#Checks that everything has been correctly done
head(philly.2014)   #Sees first 6 rows
dim(philly.2014)    #Checks dimensions of dataset
class(philly.2014)  #Checks class classification for each variable
```

```{r}
#Reads 500Cities_2017_CensusTractData.csv file
smoking.data.2017<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DannyTran0/BMIN5030_Final_Project/refs/heads/master/500Cities_2017_CensusTractData.csv")

#Visualizes data
head(smoking.data.2017)

#Filters and selects relevant variables
philly.smoking.2017<-smoking.data.2017 |>
  filter(StateAbbr=="PA", PlaceName=="Philadelphia") |>
  mutate(TractFIPS=str_pad(as.character(TractFIPS),
                           width = 11)) |>
  select(StateAbbr,PlaceName,TractFIPS,CSMOKING_CrudePrev)
  
##Checks that everything has been correctly done
head(philly.smoking.2017)
dim(philly.smoking.2017)
```

```{r}
#Loads in 2017 tract data of Philadelphia
philly.tract.2017<-tracts(state="PA",
                     county="Philadelphia",
                     year=2017) |>
  select(GEOID,geometry)

#Merges the geospatial coordinates from the 2017 tract data into smoking data using GEOID
philly.2017<-philly.tract.2017 |>
  inner_join(philly.smoking.2017,
             by=c("GEOID"="TractFIPS"))

#Checks that everything has been correctly done
head(philly.2017)
dim(philly.2017)
class(philly.2017)
```

Smoking prevalence data from 2014 and 2017 is taken and consolidated into its own table. A new column is added into the table in "philly.smoke.data.consolidation.2017" to show the change in smoking prevalence between 2014 and 2017. This is done by subtracting the smoking prevalence smoking data from 2017 (the latest data) with the one from 2014 (the older data).

```{r}
#Stores smoking prevalance data
philly.smoke.change.2014<-philly.smoking.2014$CSMOKING_CrudePrev
philly.smoke.change.2017<-philly.smoking.2017$CSMOKING_CrudePrev

philly.2017<-philly.2017 |>
#Adds a new variable about a change in smoking prevalence between 2014 and 2017
  mutate(smoke.prevalence.change=philly.smoke.change.2017-philly.smoke.change.2014)
```

## Results {#sec-results}

### Association Between Smoking and Periodontal Disease

#### Visualization of Data

To understand whether there are other factors at play that could cause a participant to smoke with the potential to develop periodontal disease, it is important to first look at what the data shows. Various demographic variables which includes their age, gender, race, and education is plotted as a bar graph relative to whether they are a current smoker or a non-smoker. Filtering was done with the age data as some of it was missing.

```{r}
#Selects the relevant variables
smoker.gender<-select(periodontal.data,gender,smoker.status)

#Creates a bar plot visualizing a participant's smoker status based on gender
ggplot(smoker.gender,aes(x=gender,fill=smoker.status))+
  geom_bar()+
#Labels the x-axis, y-axis, and title for the plot
  labs(x="Gender",y="Number of Participants",title="Smoker status of participant based on gender")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(plot.title=element_text(hjust=0.5))

#Creates a bar plot visualizing a participant's smoker status based on age
smoker.age<-select(periodontal.data,age,smoker.status) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(age)) #Filters out missing data
#Creates a bar plot visualizing a participant's smoker status based on their age
ggplot(smoker.age,aes(x=age,fill=smoker.status))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(x="Age",y="Number of Participants",title="Smoker status of participant based on age")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(plot.title=element_text(hjust=0.5))

#Creates a bar plot visualizing a participant's smoker status based on race
smoker.race<-select(periodontal.data,race,smoker.status)
#Creates a bar plot visualizing a participant's smoker status based on race
ggplot(smoker.race,aes(x=race,fill=smoker.status))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(x="Race",y="Number of Participants",title="Smoker status of participant based on race")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(plot.title=element_text(hjust=0.5))

#Creates a bar plot visualizing a participant's smoker status based on education
smoker.education<-select(periodontal.data,education,smoker.status)
#Creates a bar plot visualizing a participant's smoker status based on their education
ggplot(smoker.education,aes(x=education,fill=smoker.status))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(x="Education Level",y="Number of Participants",title="Smoker status of participant based on education")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(plot.title=element_text(hjust=0.5))
```

Visually speaking, all of the bar plots appears to shows an approximate even split between current smokers and non-smokers for each of the demographic variables. This falls in line with how the data was initially structured by the CDC by pairing a smoker and non-smoker together while preparing for analysis. For each of the demographic variables, more men were found to be smokers compared to women. In terms of age, a decrease with the number of smokers and non-smokers with age were observed. For race, participants who were labelled as "Other" vastly outnumbered African American participants 3 to 1 in terms of smoking status. Lastly, there shows an increase in the number of smokers in terms of education for the most part with a sharp decrease with participants who have gone to college.

Next, the number of detected and non-detected periodontal disease measurements were plotted on a violin plot with the participant's smoker status. The measurement for determining if periodontal disease is detected is through the 6-site periodontal charting. The process involves a thin dental probe measuring the depth of gum pockets around each tooth and if it measures to be approximately 4 mm or longer, that indicates the onset of periodontal disease \[5\].

```{r}
#Creates a violin plot on the counted number of periodontal disease measurements relative to the participant's smoker status
ggplot(periodontal.data,aes(x=smoker.status,y=peri.detected))+
  geom_violin(draw_quantiles=c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))+
  labs(x="Smoker Status",y="# of detected P.D.",title="Distribution of counted periodontal disease measurements based on smoker status")+
  theme_bw()

#Creates a violin plot on the counted number of non-periodontal disease measurements relative to the participant's smoker status
ggplot(periodontal.data,aes(x=smoker.status,y=peri.not.detected))+
  geom_violin(draw_quantiles=c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))+
  labs(x="Smoker Status",y="# of no P.D. detected",title="Distribution of counted non-periodontal disease measurements based on smoker status")+
  theme_bw()
```

From the violin plot for the count on periodontal disease measurements, it shows a large distribution of data points near 0 and narrows quickly for non-smokers, indicating little to no periodontal disease being detected. Smokers have a different distribution with a more narrower distribution at or near 0, but thickens moving upwards. This indicates that smokers were more susceptible to being diagnosed with periodontal disease.

A similar case of distribution can be said for both smokers and non-smokers with the count of no periodontal disease being measured. For smokers, the violin shape is mirrored, more thicker near the bottom, and closer to 0, showing that the number of healthy teeth is diminished and periodontal disease has progressed to large number of teeth. The distribution for non-smokers is quite different with the distribution congregating near the top of the graph. There are some thickness moving towards the bottom, indicating periodontal disease may have been discovered.

Lastly with participants who are current smokers, the number of cigarettes they use per day will be plotted on a scatterplot relative the percentage of detected periodontal disease.

```{r}
#Periodontal-smoking data stored in new variable and filtered to contain only data on participants who are current smokers
peri.filter<-Periodontal_df |>
  rename(smoker.status=z,
         percent.peri.detected=pcteither) |>
  filter(smoker.status==1) #1 indicates that participant is a current smoker

#Creates a scatterplot to compare between the percentage of periodontal disease that was detected based on the approximate number of cigarettes the participants smoked per day
ggplot(peri.filter,aes(x=percent.peri.detected,y=cigsperday))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x="Percentage of peridontal disease detected [%]",
       y="Approximate number of cigarettes per day",
       title="Percentage of peridontal disease detected based on the number of cigarettes used")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(plot.title=element_text(hjust=0.5))
```

For the most part, a relatively large distribution of data points are located near the bottom of the plot, but have varying degrees of how much of the disease has affected their set of teeth. Surprisingly, there are a few located far from this distribution in terms of the number of cigarettes being used per day with least 3 using more than 60. However, this does not say much on whether smoking too many cigarettes daily would cause the onset of the disease from happening.

#### Bi-/Multivariate Analysis

A bivariate analysis (linear model) is conducted with smoker status as the predictor variable and the percentage of periodontal disease detected as the outcome variable. Though there is data that counts the number of detected and undetected periodontal disease measurements, using the percentage of periodontal disease detected was better as it describes how much of a participant's set of teeth has been affected by the disease compared to the count of the diseased and healthy points of the teeth.

```{r}
#Bivariable Analysis

#Runs a bivariate analysis to determine the relationship between the outcome variable 
#(percentage of detected periodontal disease) and predictor variable (smoker status)
peri.smoke<-lm(percent.peri.detected~smoker.status,
                data=periodontal.data)

#Summarizes bivariate analysis data of detected periodontal disease and smoker status
summary(peri.smoke)
```

According to the bivariate analysis, it shows that there is an association with a participant's smoker status in affecting the percentage of periodontal disease being detected with a p-value p\<2e-16. This indicates that the possibility of this association being due to change is very small and that participants who currently smoke do have an influence on causing periodontal disease.

Moving from the bivariate analysis, multivariate analysis was also conducted with additional predictor variables added (age, gender, race, and education).

```{r}
#Multivariate analysis
#Runs a multivariate analysis of detected periodontal disease with smoker status, age, gender, race, and education level
periodontal.all<-lm(percent.peri.detected~smoker.status+age+gender+race+education,data=periodontal.data)

#Summarizes results of multivariate analysis
summary(periodontal.all)
```

Most of the predictor variables were found to be significantly associated with smoker status influencing the onset of periodontal disease among participants. Only a few subgroups of the education variable were found with a non-significant p-value (QED/High School, Some College, and College), indicating that participants with those education levels do not have an effect on the association between a participant's smoker status and periodontal disease.

### Exploring Changes to Smoking Prevalence

Using 2014 and 2017 census tract data, two choropleth and a leaflet map were created to visualize the prevalence of smoking in Philadelphia and any changes that occurred in a three-year period, respectively.

```{r}
#Choropleth Map

#Customizes aspects of a plot
my_theme <- function() {
  theme_minimal() +                                  
    theme(axis.line = element_blank(),                 
          axis.text = element_blank(),                 
          axis.title = element_blank(),
          panel.grid = element_line(color = "white"),  
          legend.key.size = unit(0.8, "cm"),          
          legend.text = element_text(size = 7),       
          legend.title = element_text(size = 7),
          plot.title = element_text(size = 12))      
}

#Creates a palette
myPalette<-colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(9,"YlOrRd"))

#Finds the maximum and minimum from the 2014 smoking prevalence data
prev.max.2014<-max(philly.2014$CSMOKING_CrudePrev)
prev.min.2014<-min(philly.2014$CSMOKING_CrudePrev)

#Creates a choropleth map of the smoking prevalence in Philadelphia from 2014
ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data=philly.2014,lwd=0,aes(fill=CSMOKING_CrudePrev))+
  ggtitle("Smoking Prevalence in Philadelphia in 2014")+
  scale_fill_gradientn(name="Smoking Prevalence (%)",colours=myPalette(100),limit=range(prev.max.2014,prev.min.2014))+
  my_theme()
```

```{r}
#Choropleth map

#Finds the maximum and minimum from the 2017 smoking prevalence data
prev.max.2017<-max(philly.2017$CSMOKING_CrudePrev)
prev.min.2017<-min(philly.2017$CSMOKING_CrudePrev)

#Creates a choropleth map of the smoking prevalence in Philadelphia from 2017
ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data=philly.2017,lwd=0,aes(fill=CSMOKING_CrudePrev))+
  ggtitle("Smoking Prevalence in Philadelphia in 2017")+
  scale_fill_gradientn(name="Smoking Prevalence (%)",colours=myPalette(100),limit=range(prev.max.2017,prev.min.2017))+
  my_theme()
```

Based on the choropleth maps, it shows that the high smoking prevalence is concentrated in the North and West Philadelphia areas for both 2014 and 2017. A very slight change is observed in the 2017 map, particularly with the West Philadelphia area, where there was a decrease in the smoking prevalence, but not to a great extent. In comparison, a low smoking prevalence is found in the Center City and Northwest area of Philadelphia for both years. This indicates that people living in those areas are less likely to smoke.

```{r}
#Leaflet map

#Bins continuous variables into an ordinal color scale appropriate for our data
palette.map<-colorNumeric(
  palette=c("green","yellow","red"),
  domain=philly.2017$smoke.prevalence.change
)

#Creates a pop-up message containing county name, state name, and obesity rate change as a percentage
pu.message<-paste0(philly.2017$PlaceName,
                   ", ",
                   philly.2017$StateAbbr,
                   "<br> Tract FIPS Code: ",
                   philly.2017$GEOID,
                   "<br>Change in Smoking Prevalence (2014-2017): ",
                   philly.2017$smoke.prevalence.change,
                   "%")

#Creates an interactive choropleth map of the obesity rate change in each U.S. county
leaflet(philly.2017) |>
  addPolygons(stroke=F,                       #Removes polygon borders
              fillColor=~palette.map(philly.2017$smoke.prevalence.change), 
              fillOpacity=0.7,                #Increases opacity
              smoothFactor=0.5,               #Increases resolution
              popup=pu.message) |>            #Adds pop-up message
  addLegend("bottomright",                    #Places legend in designated location
            pal=palette.map,                   #Palette function
            values=~smoke.prevalence.change,  #Variable to pass palette function
            title="Smoking Prevalence Change (%)",  #Title of legend
            opacity=1) |>                     #Legend opacity
  addScaleBar()                               #Adds distance scale
```

For the most part, there was a moderate to high drop in the smoking prevalence throughout the city which are shown in yellow and green, respectively, for part of Northwest, West, and South Philadelphia. However, there are patches of orange and red mainly in parts of North and Northeast Philadelphia, indicating an increase the number of people turning to smoking.

### Limitations

It is important to realize that all of the data used for this project is quite old, being almost or over a decade old. Therefore, conclusions made will likely be outdated or not representative of the current public health situations on smoking usage that Philadelphia may be experiencing.

Despite the periodontal-smoking dataset providing the relevant data to conduct this project, one particular result that was not properly conducted was visualizing and doing a multivariate analysis with race as a predictor variable on the association of smoking with periodontal disease detection. This is due to how the data from the R package `ForCausality` were labelled. Specifically, any race other than "African American" was labeled as "Other." It limits the conclusions that could be made with analyzing race as a predictor variable as the outcomes would be skewed and not representative of the general population.

When creating the choropleth and leaflet maps to highlight the smoking prevalence in the city, it was noticed that there were missing areas, specifically areas in South and Northeast Philadelphia. It is possible that the data in those missing areas were not reported, causing the corresponding GEOID codes to be filtered out in the code as a result while the data was processed.

## Conclusion and Future Direction

Smoking could have profound effects on a person's health and the health of those around them. However, that alone can not fully show if it is one of the primary causes of peridontal disease. But with it being a treatable disease, the city of Philadelphia should have public health responses in place to tackle smoking/tobacco use and make efforts to help current smokers get the necessary treatments.

A potential direction this project could works towards is mapping the locations of dental clinics and facilities throughout Philadelphia to compare with the smoking prevalence levels. Though no public dataset was found on the number of operating dental clinics and their location in Philadelphia, it would be beneficial to find where they are lacking. In turn, the city government and local leaders could make plans to address the problems of smoking and ensure proper care of the smoker's oral health for years to come.

Another potential direction would be to include the usage of smokeless cigarettes and e-cigarettes in the data. They are also as bad in terms of causing number health problems like periodontal disease. Including them into the analysis would further highlight the goals of this project on how smoking of any kind can bring harm to the users' health and the health of those around them.
